rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Make the gradient slightly shallower to test whether the lone critical pair gains resolution while retaining the current selectivity. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, leaving a chance to reach full credit without a time penalty.

The critical pair improved with a shallower gradient. Raising phi0 to 0.15 narrows the window and further reduces the slope while advancing elution, aiming for full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Lengthen the gradient by one step to improve the remaining critical pair, which responded positively to longer tG. The last peak is expected around 9.6 minutes, so full resolution could achieve the maximum CRF without a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already secured; increase temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved run. Holding the gradient fixed isolates whether temperature improves or compromises the critical pair.

Test whether a higher temperature separates the critical pair again after an elution-order reversal, while shortening the gradient. Injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback; this run explores a faster fully resolved alternative.

Lengthen the gradient one step at 55 C to test whether the new critical pair reaches full resolution. The last peak should remain below 9 minutes, potentially improving speed over the fully resolved method from injection 4.

Slightly narrow the gradient window to gain the small resolution improvement needed by the critical pair at 55 C. The predicted last-peak time is about 9 minutes, potentially achieving CRF 1.000 faster than injection 4.

Shift the fully resolved gradient window upward by 0.05 while preserving its slope to seek earlier elution. This tests whether the critical pairs retain sufficient selectivity and the first two peaks remain adequately retained and separated.

Return to the successful 40 C selectivity and raise phi0 one step relative to injection 4 to shorten elution. The lower temperature should improve early-peak retention compared with injection 9, while the shallower slope may preserve resolution of the central cluster.

Explore the upper temperature limit with a shorter gradient, testing whether the pair that converged at 55 C separates after reversing order. Restoring phi0 to 0.15 protects early-peak separation while seeking a substantially faster maximum-score method.

The critical pair appears to have reversed order at 60 C, so a steeper gradient may now widen rather than close its separation. Shorten tG to test this direction while retaining the starting fraction that adequately separates the early peaks.

Test an intermediate temperature with the fast gradient to balance the two temperature-sensitive central pairs. Lowering T should reopen the pair that limits the 60 C runs, while this steep gradient may maintain separation of the other central pair after its order reversal.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the pair that limited the 55 C runs, while shortening tG to keep elution fast. This tests whether the starting window can provide sufficient selectivity without the longer gradient required by injection 8.
Lengthen injection 14 by one grid step to lift its lone deficient pair above R = 1.5. The last peak should remain near 8.2 minutes, offering a faster fully resolved method than injection 8.

Use a slope between injections 14 and 15 by reducing the endpoint to 0.85 with a 12-minute gradient. This should retain full resolution while bringing the last peak slightly earlier than the current fastest fully resolved run.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 16 while keeping the endpoint above the observed elution window. Interpolation predicts the critical pairs will remain above R = 1.5, with the last peak near 7.75 minutes.

The fastest fully resolved method so far is injection 17; now test lower-temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient. Cooling may separate the central cluster in a different order, offering a faster alternative without risking loss of late peaks.

Return to the favorable 55 C selectivity and lower phi0 to improve the pair limiting injection 14. The wider, steeper gradient should keep the last peak near 7.6 minutes; the key test is whether the other central pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 17 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at phi0 = 0.10. The critical pair is expected near R = 1.5, with the last peak around 7.6 minutes; injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Increase the slope modestly relative to injection 19 to test the faster boundary at the lowest starting organic fraction. This should shorten elution, but the central pairs may lose full resolution; injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed CRF 1.000 method.

Test a faster, higher-starting-organic method at 50 C, where early peaks should retain more separation than at 55 C. The shifted window may balance the two central selectivity-sensitive pairs; injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved fallback.

Test the unmeasured 35 C selectivity with a gradient shorter than the successful 40 C method. This may improve the original critical pair, though neighboring pairs could become limiting; injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 19’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its gradient slope through the observed elution window. All peaks should still elute before the gradient ends, retaining CRF 1.000 and the approximately 7.6-minute last-peak time with a shorter programmed gradient.

Preserve injection 16’s fully resolving slope while trimming the unused gradient tail; its last peak should still elute before the gradient ends at the outlet. This targets CRF 1.000 with slightly more resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method, which remains injection 24.
